Legacy taxonomy.json note for aws:iam-user-secret-access-key (verbatim legacy text; the date is the dossier researchedAt, not the authoring date): Registry detector aws-secret-access-key since redact-secret#1028 (registry pin 4fb7882). Contract in benchmarks/lib/beta8/1012a.ts from the #1012 research record: T2, context-constrained (exactly 40 [A-Za-z0-9/+] only under an AWS secret key name or next to an AKIA access key id); the value has no prefix, so no bare-value claim is made.

Legacy contract review text for 'aws-secret-access-key' (verbatim legacy text; the date is the dossier researchedAt, not the authoring date): Context-gated registry family (#1012 READY-T2, context-constrained; product redact-secret#1028, a registry detector since the 4fb7882 pin). The secret half of a long-term IAM user access key: with its AKIA id it signs any API call the user may make. T2: exactly 40 [A-Za-z0-9/+] is the AWS docs example shape (R5) and the grammar of two AWS-owned scanner rules (git-secrets, ferret-scan; R2 would make them T1 but is not applied) and of peers from Truffle Security, Praetorian and Google; no AWS page states "40 characters" in prose. The value has no prefix, and AWS's own detectors require context (Macie: "Keyword required: Yes"), so the family is recognised only under an AWS secret key name (aws_secret_access_key, AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY, SecretAccessKey, secret_access_key, aws_secret_key, "secret access key") or next to an AKIA access key id; its positives score as project policy and its context twins keep the value byte-for-byte and remove that gate. = inside the 40 is excluded (30 random bytes encode to 40 characters without padding; ferret-scan, trufflehog and veles agree). Excluded: a bare 40-character run, temporary (ASIA-paired) secrets (the only AWS example is 41 characters), and session tokens. No fixture asserts silence on a 40-character Base64 value beside the gate: the contract admits any such value there.
